newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK says GDP growth may slow if China loses MFN.
newsitem.headline: HK says GDP growth may slow if China loses MFN.

text.p: Hong Kong's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate may slow by 2.0 to 2.8 percentage points if China loses its most favoured nation (MFN) trading privileges in the United States, the government said on Friday.
That represented a drop of two-fifths to three-fifths from its trend rate of five percent annually, Acting Secretary for Trade and Industry Tam Wing-pong said in a statement.
Annual GDP growth came in at 4.7 percent in each of the last two years, and is forecast at 5.5 percent for 1997.
The terrritory's re-exports from China to the United States might fall by 32 to 45 percent, or by HK$73 billion to HK$103 billion (US$9.4 billion to US$13.3 billion), Tam said.

Together with other related trade flows, there might be a reduction of six to eight percent, or HK$174 billion to HK$246 billion, in Hong Kong's overall trade, with a loss of about HK$24 billion to HK$34 billion in income and some 61,000 to 86,000 jobs as a direct impact, he said.
"There would be a further loss in income and jobs if China cut back on its imports from the U.S. as a result," Tam said.

"Manufacturing investments and other production arrangements by Hong Kong and foreign companies in China would also be adversely affected," he said. Tam said he was concerned that Hong Kong's role as a gateway to China would be undermined, thereby affecting longer term growth potential and business confidence in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong serves as an entrepot for China, and many Hong Kong manufacturers have moved their production bases to China to take advantage of lower production costs.
Tam envisaged a lively debate in the U.S. Congress over the renewal of China's MFN status this year.
"The situation is complex this year as Hong Kong's transition will likely be in the limelight when Congress debates on China's MFN renewal," he said.
Britains hands Hong Kong back to China at midnight of June 30, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule.
"The climate is also affected by the overall Sino-U.S. relations, but we shall argue strongly that the MFN issue should not be linked with non-trade issues," he said.
Tam said 1997 was a more critical year for Hong Kong's development than any since annual MFN renewal debates began.
"A steady economy is vital for our successful transition. We will do our utmost to get our message across," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has until June to decide on MFN, and Congress then must decide whether to overturn that decision.
